title: The rainmakers, 1946
teaches: How dry ice and silver iodide trigger snowfall in a supercooled cloud, how dosing controls crystal growth, which clouds seeding can and cannot help, and how randomized trials separate a real effect from a lucky winter.

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: Most clouds between 0 °C and −20 °C are **supercooled**: liquid droplets colder than freezing, waiting for a template speck to initiate ice. Once ice crystals appear, they grow rapidly at the droplets’ expense and fall as snow. What holds back precipitation in such a cloud is a shortage of ice, not water.
**Dry ice** (−78 °C) triggers freezing by sheer cold in any cloud below 0 °C. **Silver iodide** acts as a crystal template whose atomic lattice mimics ice, working in clouds colder than about −5 °C.

Seeding a cloud layer with the right concentration of crystals snows a clear hole in it. Too few crystals produce only scattered flurries; too many split the water among millions of crystals too tiny to fall (**overseeding**).

Seeding cannot create clouds or moisture from clear air. It operates inside a specific temperature window (roughly −5 °C to −25 °C), reliably clearing supercooled airport fog and adding modest snowfall (about 5–15%) to suitable winter mountain clouds.

Natural storm totals vary so wildly that only a **randomized trial**—comparing randomly seeded storms against unseeded control storms across many winters—can prove whether seeding actually added snow.

blocks.text: Lesson 7 introduced a striking quirk of cloud physics: most clouds between 0 °C and −20 °C consist of liquid droplets colder than freezing (**supercooled** water). A microscopic droplet freezes above −38 °C only if it touches an **ice nucleus**—a solid speck whose atomic lattice templates the six-sided geometry of ice. Although every litre of outdoor air holds millions of condensation specks (salt, dust, sulphate), almost none of them have the right crystal geometry to start ice.

Consider a litre of cloud air at −10 °C. It typically holds around 100,000 supercooled liquid droplets, yet natural ice nuclei active at −10 °C average only about one speck per 250 litres. As the cloud grows colder, more mineral dust specks become active—roughly tenfold for every 4 °C drop in temperature—but even at −15 °C there is still only about one active ice nucleus per dozen litres of cloud. A cloud deck in that temperature range can linger for hours, brimming with liquid water that cannot fall simply because it lacks ice crystals.

blocks.caption: The scarcity of natural ice nuclei compared to supercooled liquid droplets in a litre of cloud.

blocks.text: Once a few ice crystals do appear, Lesson 7’s vapour-scavenging engine (the Bergeron process) takes over: water vapour deposits rapidly onto the ice while surrounding supercooled droplets evaporate to feed them, growing heavy snowflakes within 15 to 20 minutes. In a supercooled cloud between −5 °C and −20 °C, precipitation is bottlenecked not by a shortage of water, but by a shortage of ice. That bottleneck is the entire premise of **cloud seeding**: supply the missing ice crystals.

In 1946, at the General Electric Research Laboratory in Schenectady, New York, self-taught researcher Vincent Schaefer was working alongside Nobel laureate Irving Langmuir to study aircraft icing—how supercooled cloud droplets freeze on contact with aeroplane wings. To study supercooled clouds indoors, Schaefer built a simple cloud chamber.

He lined an ordinary commercial chest freezer with black velvet, chilled it to −15 °C, and breathed into it. The moisture in his breath condensed into a miniature cloud of supercooled droplets. A narrow beam from a microscope lamp shone across the dark interior so that any ice crystals would flash like tiny diamonds against the black velvet. For months, Schaefer dusted the cloud with talc, salt, sulphur, volcanic ash, and ground minerals, searching for a powder that would trigger freezing. Almost nothing worked at mild sub-freezing temperatures.

On a hot afternoon in July 1946, the freezer unit was struggling to stay cold enough, so Schaefer placed a chunk of **dry ice** inside to chill the chamber. The instant his breath met the air above the dry ice, the light beam exploded with millions of glittering ice crystals, which grew at the expense of the fog and settled to the floor of the freezer as miniature snow.

blocks.caption: Schaefer’s cold-box experiment: a chest freezer filled with supercooled cloud and side-lit by a lamp. Set the temperature, then test different seeding agents.
blocks.task: Make it snow in the box.

blocks.text: Test each substance across several temperatures in the interactive freezer. Above 0 °C, nothing works—not even dry ice—because the droplets are warm water and any ice crystals melt immediately. Below 0 °C, natural soil dust nucleates a handful of crystals only when the box is colder than about −12 °C. **Silver iodide** smoke does nothing between 0 °C and −4 °C, then suddenly fills the box with crystals once cooled past −5 °C. **Dry ice** triggers a blizzard at every temperature below 0 °C.

Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide at **−78.5 °C**. Unlike a mineral speck, it does not act as a crystal template; it works by brute thermal shock. As a pellet of dry ice falls through a supercooled cloud, it chills a thin wake of air directly behind it well below **−40 °C**—cold enough for supercooled droplets in that wake to freeze spontaneously without needing any speck at all (and for water vapour to condense and freeze directly into ice[^deposition]).

blocks.caption: How a falling pellet of dry ice (−78.5 °C) freezes a trail of billions of microscopic ice crystals in its wake.

blocks.text: A single gram of falling dry ice leaves hundreds of billions of microscopic ice embryos trailing in its wake. As turbulent air mixes those newly formed crystals outward into the surrounding supercooled cloud, they scavenge vapour from the liquid droplets and grow into snow—working in any cloud layer colder than 0 °C.

Dry ice has a practical limitation, however: it must be carried aloft by an aircraft and dropped directly into the top of the cloud, and its pellets sublimate completely after falling a kilometre or two.

On 13 November 1946, Schaefer took off from Schenectady in a light aeroplane, flew east toward Mount Greylock in Massachusetts, and scattered three pounds of crushed dry ice along a five-kilometer line through a supercooled stratocumulus deck at −20 °C. Within five minutes, the cloud along his flight track transformed into long curtains of falling snow that carved a trough right through the cloud deck. Although the snow evaporated as virga in the dry air below before reaching the ground, Schaefer had demonstrated for the first time that human intervention could trigger precipitation in a natural cloud.

Meanwhile, atmospheric physicist Bernard Vonnegut—working down the hall at General Electric[^vonnegut]—pursued the template problem. If natural dust specks rarely trigger freezing because their atomic spacing poorly matches ice, could a chemist find a synthetic crystal whose atomic lattice matches hexagonal ice almost perfectly?

Combing through X-ray crystallography tables, Vonnegut spotted **silver iodide (AgI)**. Like ice, silver iodide forms a six-sided hexagonal crystal, and the spacing between its atoms (0.459 nanometres) sits within **1.5 percent** of the spacing between water molecules in ice (0.452 nanometres). When a supercooled droplet touches a microscopic speck of silver iodide, the water molecules lock onto that hexagonal scaffold almost as easily as onto ice itself. Tested in the cold box in November 1946, a tiny spark of silver iodide smoke filled the chamber with glittering snow.

Silver iodide offers two major operational advantages over dry ice. First, a tiny mass generates an astronomical number of nuclei: burning a single gram of silver iodide in an acetone flame produces roughly 10¹⁵ (a quadrillion) microscopic smoke particles—thousands of times more crystals per gram than dry ice. Second, because silver iodide particles do not evaporate in warm air, they can be released from flares on aircraft or from ground-based generators placed upwind of a mountain range, letting natural upslope winds carry the smoke plumes up into the supercooled cloud deck.

blocks.caption: Two ways to deliver ice nuclei into an orographic cloud: ground-based silver iodide generators carried upslope by mountain winds, or aircraft dropping flares/dry ice from above.

blocks.text: Silver iodide’s one limitation comes from that 1.5 percent lattice mismatch. Whereas a seed crystal of real ice freezes supercooled water immediately below 0 °C, the slight atomic mismatch of silver iodide requires the water to be supercooled to at least **−4 °C or −5 °C** before water molecules lock onto the template (and it becomes much more efficient below −8 °C to −10 °C). In a mildly supercooled layer sitting at −2 °C, dry ice works instantly while silver iodide does nothing.

parts.title: Opening a hole in the sky

blocks.text: What happens when an entire layer of supercooled cloud is seeded? Because the cloud holds a fixed supply of liquid water, the outcome depends entirely on how many ice crystals have to share that water. Early flight trials found that scattering roughly one pound of crushed dry ice per mile of flight produced an ideal concentration of about 10 to 100 ice crystals per litre of cloud.

If a cloud is **underseeded** (fewer than one crystal per litre), each crystal has plenty of water vapour to itself and grows into a heavy snowflake that falls out, but there are too few crystals to consume the cloud deck; a few flurries fall and the cloud layer remains intact. At the **optimal dose** (roughly 10 to 1,000 crystals per litre), the crystals rapidly consume all the supercooled droplets, grow heavy enough to fall out as snow within 20 to 30 minutes, and punch a clear **fallstreak hole** right through the cloud deck.

If a cloud is injected with far too many nuclei (several thousand crystals per litre), the available liquid water gets divided among so many competing crystals that no single crystal can grow heavy enough to fall. The supercooled liquid layer simply converts into a persistent, wispy cloud of tiny ice crystals that hangs aloft without snowing—a mistake known as **overseeding**.

blocks.caption: Seeding a supercooled cloud deck from above. The gauges below show crystal concentration per litre and resulting snowflake size.
blocks.task: Seed the layer just enough to snow a hole in it.

blocks.text: Even when seeding successfully snows out a cloud layer aloft, getting that precipitation all the way to the ground requires two things: the cloud must be thick enough to hold a meaningful supply of liquid water, and the air beneath the cloud base must be humid enough that the falling snow doesn't evaporate into virga on the way down.

Watching a pass with dry ice carve a five-kilometre hole through a cloud deck in thirty minutes made headlines in 1946 and sparked bold claims that humanity would soon end droughts and steer hurricanes. Understanding the physical limits of cloud seeding is just as important as understanding how it works.

First, **seeding cannot create clouds or moisture**. It can only trigger freezing inside an existing cloud that already contains supercooled liquid water. In a clear sky, seeding agents have nothing to work on.

During a summer drought, skies stay stubbornly clear because a stationary high-pressure system is pressing air downward, warming and drying it by compression (Lesson 2). Forming a rain cloud requires lifting humid air to its dew point (Lesson 1), and no amount of silver iodide smoke can lift an air mass.

Second, as Lesson 2 showed, a cloud layer holds very little water at any single instant—typically around 0.2 millimetres of rainfall equivalent per kilometre of depth. Substantial precipitation only happens when a storm system continuously lifts fresh moist air through the cloud like a conveyor belt. Seeding can only nudge that conveyor belt to convert a slightly higher fraction of its passing supercooled liquid into snow before the air flows past.

Third, seeding only helps inside a specific **temperature window**. In clouds warmer than **0 °C**, neither dry ice nor silver iodide works because no supercooled water exists.[^hygroscopic] Between **0 °C and −5 °C**, only dry ice (or venting liquid propane) works because silver iodide requires at least 5 °C of supercooling. The productive **seeding window** sits between roughly **−5 °C and −25 °C**, where supercooled water is abundant and natural ice nuclei are still scarce.

Colder than about **−25 °C**, nature no longer needs help: natural mineral dust specks become active in such large numbers that the cloud already produces plenty of its own ice crystals. And below **−38 °C**, every remaining liquid droplet freezes spontaneously. Adding artificial nuclei to a cloud colder than −25 °C simply risks overseeding it.

blocks.caption: The temperature window for glaciogenic cloud seeding. In summer, the 0 °C level sits ~3–4 km high; in winter, it can sit near the valley floor.

blocks.text: That temperature window explains why summer cumulus clouds over dry basins are poor targets: small fair-weather puffs sit entirely below the freezing level (warmer than 0 °C), while towering afternoon thunderstorms quickly punch into the −25 °C to −40 °C zone and generate tons of natural ice on their own.
Instead, glaciogenic seeding works reliably in two cold-season settings: **supercooled winter fog** in valleys, and **winter orographic clouds** forced up mountain barriers.

**Clearing supercooled airport fog** is cloud seeding’s most unambiguous operational success. When sub-freezing fog (−2 °C to −15 °C) shuts down a winter runway, spraying expanding liquid propane from ground nozzles (which chills the air at the nozzle below −40 °C) or dropping crushed dry ice from a light plane floods the fog bank with ice crystals. Within 30 to 45 minutes, the crystals scavenge the fog droplets, settle out as a light dusting of snow, and open a clear visibility corridor over the runway. (In fog warmer than 0 °C, however, the technique does nothing at all.)

blocks.caption: Seeding supercooled freezing fog upwind of an airport runway precipitates the fog droplets as fine snow, opening a clear landing slot.

blocks.text: **Winter mountain (orographic) snowpack** is the other proven application. When moist winter winds blow up a mountain barrier like the Cascades, Sierra Nevada, or Rockies, the air cools and condenses into a supercooled cloud bank along the windward slope. Because the air crosses the ridge crest in less than an hour, natural ice crystals often don't have enough time to form and snow out before the air plunges down the leeward side and evaporates in the rain shadow (Lesson 7).

Releasing silver iodide upwind of the ridge starts ice-crystal growth earlier on the windward climb, allowing more snowflakes to grow heavy enough to fall onto the high peaks before the air spills over the crest. Multi-year studies indicate that under the right conditions (−5 °C to −20 °C cloud tops with supercooled liquid present), winter orographic seeding can boost snowfall from individual seeded storms by **5 to 15 percent**—storing extra snowpack at high elevation that melts into summer river runoff.

Attempts to seed **severe hailstorms** (to create more, smaller hailstones by competing for supercooled water) or **hurricanes** (to weaken eyewall winds) have never demonstrated a clear, reproducible success in randomized trials. Violent storms process such immense volumes of water and natural ice that artificial seeding disappears into the natural variability of the storm.[^stormfury]
That brings us to the hardest problem in weather modification: if you seed a cloud and it snows 10 millimetres, how do you know it wouldn't have snowed 10 millimetres on its own?

Natural storm-to-storm variability is huge. One winter storm crossing a mountain range may drop 40 millimetres of water equivalent while the next drops 4 millimetres. A true seeding boost of 10 percent is completely invisible inside a single storm—or even a single wet or dry winter.

The only rigorous way to measure a 10 percent signal buried in 300 percent natural noise is the same method medicine uses to test a new drug: a **randomized controlled trial**.[^trial] Whenever a suitable winter storm approaches with supercooled liquid in the −5 °C to −20 °C window, a sealed randomizer (essentially a coin toss) decides whether to turn the silver iodide generators on or leave them off, while snow gauges in the target mountain basin—and in an upwind **control basin** that is never seeded—measure the snowfall blinded to the decision. Only after comparing dozens of seeded storms against dozens of unseeded storms across five to ten winters does natural luck average out enough to reveal the true seeding effect.

blocks.caption: A simulated multi-winter seeding trial where seeding genuinely adds +15% snow. Each dot is one storm's precipitation (on a logarithmic scale); the bottom bar tracks the estimated seeding ratio and its uncertainty band.
blocks.task: Run winters until the difference stands out from luck.

blocks.text: Run the interactive trial for just one or two winters and click **New winters** a few times: random luck alone can make a +15% seeding program look as if it doubled the snowpack—or as if it *reduced* the snowpack by 20%. Now toggle on **Seeder picks the storms**: when an operator chooses which storms look promising to seed instead of flipping a coin, they naturally pick the juiciest storms that were going to dump heavy snow anyway, producing a bogus 40% to 60% 'gain' that is pure **selection bias**.

Commercial rainmakers exploited that exact selection bias for generations before 1946. The most famous, Charles Hatfield, was hired by the city of San Diego during a drought in December 1915 to evaporate a 'secret chemical mixture' from towers near the Morena Reservoir.[^hatfield] Watching the barometer and high cloud signs, rainmakers waited until a Pacific storm system was already approaching, sent up their fumes, and claimed credit when the sky opened up.

For seventy years after Schaefer's 1946 flight, scientists could measure statistical gains over many winters or watch holes open in thin clouds, but they could not directly trace seeded snowflakes inside a deep mountain storm from the generator plume to the ground. In 2017, the **SNOWIE** field campaign in the Payette Mountains of Idaho combined airborne cloud radar, polarization Doppler radar, and snow gauges while an aircraft flew back-and-forth tracks releasing silver iodide into supercooled mountain clouds. For the first time, high-resolution radar captured distinct zig-zag lines of newly formed ice crystals blooming exclusively along the aircraft’s seeding tracks, growing into snow plumes that drifted downwind and registered in surface gauges.[^snowie] Even with that direct physical proof, on many storm days natural snowfall was heavy enough to swamp the seeded lines—confirming that seeding is a modest nudge in specific clouds, never a weather switch.

blocks.caption: Plan-view radar reflectivity from the 2017 SNOWIE experiment in Idaho: an aircraft flying crosswind legs releases silver iodide, producing distinct plumes of snow that drift downwind across the mountains.

blocks.text: When someone asks whether cloud seeding can 'make it rain,' you now have the physics to give an honest answer: no one can manufacture clouds out of dry, sinking air, but when nature supplies a supercooled cloud that is short of ice between −5 °C and −25 °C, adding nuclei can help wring a little extra snow or rain out of the passing air.

Answering that single question draws on every lesson in this guide: how rising air cools to its dew point (Lesson 1), why stability and cloud depth govern precipitation (Lesson 2), how temperature defines the three cloud floors (Lesson 3), how frontal systems lift wide cloud decks (Lessons 4 and 6), how latent heat drives updraughts (Lesson 5), and how supercooled droplets feed growing ice crystals over mountain ranges (Lesson 7).

blocks.title: Before you seed, ask
points: **Is there a cloud?** Seeding cannot lift air or create cloud droplets in clear, sinking air.

**Is it supercooled inside the −5 °C to −25 °C window?** Above 0 °C, nothing works; from 0 °C to −5 °C, only dry ice/propane works; colder than −25 °C, abundant natural ice nuclei already freeze the cloud.
**Will the snow survive to the ground?** The cloud layer must be deep enough to grow heavy flakes, and the sub-cloud air humid enough that they don't evaporate as virga.
**Is the dose right?** Tens of crystals per litre snow out the layer; thousands per litre **overseed** it into tiny crystals that stay suspended.
**How is it evaluated?** Only a multi-winter **randomized trial** with unseeded control storms can separate a 5–15% gain from natural storm variability and selection bias.

blocks.text: Because seeding requires supercooled liquid clouds, start by placing each photographed cloud on its floor—remembering that in winter, even low-floor clouds can sit below 0 °C. Then evaluate each seeding scenario below.

blocks.caption: Real photos to place on their floors, then a sky to seed, or not. What would seeding do?

items.question: A supercooled cloud sits at −3 °C. Which will make it snow?
options: Silver iodide, which gives the droplets a crystal to copy
Neither: at −3 °C the droplets are too warm to freeze
Dry ice, which makes its own ice crystals by sheer cold
items.why: Dry ice works at any temperature below freezing: it chills the air so much that crystals form by themselves. Silver iodide does not wake up until about −5 °C or colder.

items.question: On a hot July afternoon, fair-weather cumulus heaps have bases at 1.5 km and tops at 2.5 km. The 0 °C freezing level sits at 4 km altitude. Will dropping dry ice pellets into these clouds produce rain?
options: Yes: at −78 °C, dry ice is cold enough to freeze any cloud regardless of ambient temperature
No: the clouds sit entirely below the freezing level (warmer than 0 °C), so any ice crystals melt immediately
Yes, provided the pilot uses silver iodide flares instead of dry ice
items.why: Glaciogenic seeding requires supercooled liquid water (colder than 0 °C) so new ice crystals can grow via the Bergeron process. In a cloud warmer than 0 °C, ice crystals created in the wake of a dry ice pellet melt within seconds.

items.question: Eager for maximum snow, a pilot dumps 100 pounds of crushed dry ice per mile into a thin, supercooled stratocumulus deck at −10 °C. The cloud turns bright, silky white, but not a single snowflake falls. What went wrong?
options: The dry ice sublimated above the cloud before reaching the droplets
At −10 °C, the cloud was too warm for dry ice to nucleate ice crystals
Overseeding: the cloud's water was split among so many billions of crystals that none grew heavy enough to fall
items.why: Injecting thousands of crystals per litre splits the available liquid water among too many competing crystals (**overseeding**), turning the droplet deck into a persistent ice veil of tiny crystals that cannot fall. About 1 pound per mile is the right dose.

items.question: A supercooled stratus deck has lingered over the basin for three days at −8 °C, coating every fence wire in white rime. A local crop-duster pilot has 200 pounds of crushed dry ice on board. Can he clear a hole in the overcast?
options: Yes: the rime proves the cloud is supercooled liquid—seed it lightly at about a pound per mile
No: dry ice only works in towering summer cumulus clouds
No: at −8 °C, the cloud is already frozen solid into ice crystals
items.why: Feathery rime on fences confirms that the stratus deck consists of supercooled liquid droplets at −8 °C—ideal for dry ice (or silver iodide) seeding, provided the pilot doses it lightly (~1 lb/mile) to avoid overseeding.

items.question: After an aircraft seeds a middle-level altostratus deck at −12 °C, you watch long grey curtains of snow trail out of the cloud base along the flight path, but the ground stays completely dry. Did the seeding fail to freeze the cloud?
options: Yes: if no snow reached the ground, no ice crystals formed in the cloud
No: the seeding successfully turned the supercooled cloud into snow, but dry air below evaporated the flakes into virga
The snowflakes were blown hundreds of kilometres away before falling out of the cloud
items.why: Hanging curtains of snow that fade before reaching the ground are virga. Just as in Schaefer’s first flight over Mount Greylock in 1946, the seeding worked inside the cloud, but the sub-cloud air was too dry to let the snow reach the surface.

items.question: Six weeks into a summer drought under a stationary high-pressure ridge, the sky holds only a few flat cumulus humilis puffs at noon. A commercial rainmaker offers to bring the county a soaking rain for $2,000 using ground-based silver iodide burners. Should the Grange hire him?
options: Yes: silver iodide smoke draws moisture out of dry air to build rain clouds
Yes, as long as he runs the burners at night when the ground is cooler
No: sinking air in the high prevents deep, supercooled clouds from forming, leaving nothing to seed
items.why: Seeding cannot lift air or create clouds under a dry high-pressure inversion, nor can it work on shallow, warm cumulus puffs that never reach the −5 °C threshold required by silver iodide.

items.question: A medical flight needs to land at the town airfield, which is socked in by dense freezing fog at −7 °C with rime on the wind-sock frame. Can cloud seeding open the runway?
options: No: valley fog cannot be modified once it forms
Only if a cold front arrives to mix the inversion away
Yes: seeding the upwind fog with dry ice or expanding propane will precipitate the droplets as fine snow and clear a slot
items.why: Clearing supercooled fog (colder than 0 °C, confirmed by rime) is cloud seeding’s most reliable operational success: dry ice or expanding propane nucleates ice crystals that scavenge the fog droplets and snow out within 30 to 45 minutes.

items.question: A commercial seeder hand-picked five promising winter storms to seed last season and reported that those five storms dropped 40 percent more snow than the winter's average storm. Does this prove his seeding added 40 percent?
options: No: hand-picking promising storms introduces selection bias, and five storms are far too few to overcome natural variability
Yes: a 40 percent difference is too large to happen by chance or storm selection
Yes, provided he used silver iodide generators rather than dry ice
items.why: When an operator chooses which storms to seed, they pick strong, moisture-rich storms that would have produced heavy snow anyway (selection bias). Proving a real 5–15% seeding effect requires a randomized trial across many winters.

learned: Because active ice nuclei are scarce between 0 °C and −20 °C, clouds in this zone remain supercooled liquid for hours; once ice crystals are introduced, they rapidly scavenge vapour from the droplets (the Bergeron process) and fall as snow.

Dry ice (−78.5 °C) freezes a wake of droplets by extreme cold (< −40 °C) in any cloud below 0 °C; silver iodide has a hexagonal crystal lattice within 1.5% of ice, acting as a template speck in clouds colder than ~−5 °C and allowing dispersion from ground burners.

Dosing controls the outcome: ~10–1,000 crystals per litre snows out a supercooled layer and opens a hole, whereas injecting thousands per litre splits the water into crystals too tiny to fall (overseeding).

Seeding cannot create clouds or moisture. It works inside a −5 °C to −25 °C window, reliably clearing supercooled airport fog and adding roughly 5–15% snow to suitable winter mountain clouds, with no proven effect on droughts, hailstorms, or hurricanes.

Because natural storm totals vary wildly, only a multi-winter randomized trial—comparing randomly seeded storms against unseeded control storms—can separate a genuine seeding effect from luck and selection bias.
next: That completes the field guide. Step outside—the sky is yours to read.

supercooled.title: Clouds waiting for ice
supercooled.text: Most clouds between 0 °C and −20 °C consist of supercooled liquid droplets because natural ice nuclei active at those temperatures are scarce—roughly 1 per 250 litres at −10 °C compared to 100,000 droplets per litre. Once ice crystals appear, they grow rapidly at the droplets' expense via the Bergeron process and fall as snow. Cloud seeding works by supplying those missing ice crystals.

dry-ice.title: Dry ice
dry-ice.text: Solid carbon dioxide at −78.5 °C. Dropped from an aircraft into a supercooled cloud, a falling pellet chills a narrow wake below −40 °C, spontaneously freezing hundreds of billions of tiny ice crystals per gram without needing template specks. It works in any cloud colder than 0 °C. Discovered by Vincent Schaefer in July 1946 and first tested over Mount Greylock, Massachusetts, on 13 November 1946.

silver-iodide.title: Silver iodide
silver-iodide.text: A hexagonal crystal (AgI) whose atomic spacing (0.459 nm) matches the lattice of ice (0.452 nm) to within 1.5%, acting as a synthetic template for freezing. Active below about −5 °C (and most effective below −10 °C), a single gram burned into smoke yields ~10^15 ice-nucleating specks that can be carried into mountain clouds by updraughts from ground generators. Discovered by Bernard Vonnegut in November 1946.

overseeding.title: Seeding a layer
overseeding.text: Seeded ice crystals share a cloud's finite supply of liquid water. Too few crystals (< 1/litre) produce only light flurries; an optimal dose (~10–1,000/litre, or ~1 lb of dry ice per mile flown) rapidly converts the droplets into snowflakes that fall out and punch a hole; too many crystals (thousands/litre) divide the water so thinly that no crystal grows heavy enough to fall, leaving a persistent ice veil (overseeding).

seeding-window.title: The seeding window
seeding-window.text: Glaciogenic seeding requires supercooled liquid water and a deficit of natural ice. Above 0 °C, ice melts immediately; from 0 °C to −5 °C, only thermal-shock agents (dry ice or expanding propane) work; from −5 °C to −25 °C, both dry ice and silver iodide work effectively; colder than −25 °C, abundant natural dust nuclei already freeze the cloud, and below −38 °C droplets freeze spontaneously.

seeding-works.title: Where seeding works
seeding-works.text: Seeding reliably clears supercooled winter fog (< 0 °C) over airport runways within 30–45 minutes. In winter orographic clouds over mountain barriers, silver iodide seeding can boost snowfall by roughly 5–15% in suitable storms (−5 °C to −20 °C with supercooled liquid present and humid sub-cloud air). Randomized trials have found no clear evidence that seeding tames hailstorms or weakens hurricanes.

fair-trial.title: A fair trial
fair-trial.text: Because natural precipitation varies by hundreds of percent from storm to storm, operational claims based on hand-picked storms suffer from severe selection bias. Measuring a 5–15% seeding effect requires a randomized controlled trial across many winters, using a coin toss to decide which eligible storms are seeded and comparing target gauges against an unseeded upwind control basin.

deposition.title: Deposition and sublimation
deposition.text: When water vapour turns directly into solid ice without passing through a liquid phase—as when frost feathers grow on a cold windowpane or snowflakes grow in a cloud—physicists call the phase change **deposition**. The reverse process, solid ice turning directly into vapour without melting, is **sublimation**: it is how snowbanks slowly shrink on a cold, dry, sunny winter day, and how dry ice pellets vanish into carbon dioxide gas at −78.5 °C.

vonnegut.title: Kurt Vonnegut and 'Ice-nine'
vonnegut.text: Bernard Vonnegut’s younger brother, the novelist Kurt Vonnegut, worked in General Electric’s public relations department in Schenectady right when Schaefer, Langmuir, and Bernard were seeding clouds. In his satirical novel *Cat’s Cradle* (1963), Kurt inverted his brother’s discovery into *ice-nine*—a fictional polymorph of water that freezes at room temperature (45.8 °C) and acts as a seed crystal that locks all the world’s oceans solid on contact.

hygroscopic.title: Warm-cloud (hygroscopic) seeding
hygroscopic.text: While classic cloud seeding targets supercooled clouds with ice nuclei (*glaciogenic seeding*), a separate technique called **hygroscopic seeding** targets warm clouds (> 0 °C) by burning salt flares near cloud base. The large salt particles (1–5 micrometres wide) condense oversized 'collector drops' intended to kick-start the collision–coalescence process (Lesson 2), though proving its net effect on rainfall remains statistically challenging.

stormfury.title: Project Stormfury
stormfury.text: Between 1962 and 1983, the US government’s **Project Stormfury** flew hurricane-hunter aircraft into Atlantic hurricanes to dump silver iodide into the outer rainbands, hoping that latent heat released by freezing would build a wider eyewall and weaken the storm's peak winds. Subsequent aircraft measurements revealed why the hypothesis failed: hurricane eyewalls already contain very little supercooled liquid water and huge quantities of natural ice, and the observed wind changes were completely natural **eyewall replacement cycles**.

trial.title: Randomized controlled trials
trial.text: In a **randomized controlled trial**, eligible storm periods are assigned by chance (randomization) to either treatment (seeded) or **control** (unseeded), preventing forecasters from cherry-picking vigorous storms (*selection bias*). A result is judged **statistically significant** when the observed difference between seeded and unseeded storms is large enough that random luck alone would produce it less than 5% of the time (p < 0.05).

hatfield.title: Charles Hatfield and the $10,000 flood
hatfield.text: In December 1915, the parched city of San Diego verbally promised self-styled 'Moisture Accelerator' Charles Hatfield $10,000 if he could fill the Morena Reservoir. Hatfield erected towers and evaporated a secret chemical blend just as two historic back-to-back Pacific cyclones slammed into Southern California in January 1916. The deluge overflowed the reservoir, burst the Lower Otay Dam, destroyed bridges, and killed around 20 people. Facing $3.5 million in flood lawsuits, the city offered a deal: it would pay Hatfield his $10,000 if he accepted legal liability for the flood damage. Hatfield declined and left empty-handed.

snowie.title: The SNOWIE radar breakthrough (2017)
snowie.text: Sponsored by the US National Science Foundation, the 2017 **SNOWIE** project (*Seeded and Natural Orographic Wintertime Clouds: the Idaho Experiment*) used airborne W-band cloud radar and ground X-band Doppler radars to watch silver iodide plumes inside supercooled mountain clouds over Idaho’s Payette Basin. By flying crosswind zig-zag tracks, researchers imaged distinct lines of ice crystals nucleating, growing into snow, and falling into gauges along the exact wind-drifted aircraft path.
